Before we start, a quick note about Friday's field trip. We'll be riding the new light-rail line from one end to the other to observe how the stations connect to the neighborhoods around them. Please meet at the University Avenue stop at eight-fifteen, not here in the classroom. The department is covering your fares, so you don't need to buy tickets. Bring a notebook, because you'll be sketching at least two station layouts, and those sketches will count toward your participation grade.

Today let's look at a puzzle that confused geologists for a long time. Across parts of northern Europe and North America, you can find huge boulders sitting alone in the middle of flat fields. Some are the size of a house. What's strange is that they're often made of a completely different type of rock from the ground underneath them. A granite boulder resting on limestone, for instance. These are called glacial erratics. Early naturalists offered all sorts of explanations. Some thought volcanoes had thrown the rocks out; others believed great floods had carried them. The real answer turned out to be ice. During the last ice age, enormous glaciers moved slowly across the land. As they moved, they picked up rock, sometimes in pieces weighing thousands of tons, and carried it, in some cases, hundreds of kilometers. When the climate warmed and the ice melted, the rocks were simply left behind. Now, here's why erratics matter to geologists today. Because each type of rock comes from a particular place, an erratic acts a bit like a return address on a letter. If we can match a boulder's minerals to a known rock formation far away, we learn which direction the ice was moving. Put enough of these together, and you get a map of how ancient ice sheets flowed. One caution, though: some boulders were moved more than once, by more than one glacier, so a single erratic can be misleading on its own.

Let's continue with circadian rhythms, the roughly twenty-four-hour cycle that tells your body when to feel alert and when to feel sleepy. One of the hormones involved is melatonin. As evening approaches, the brain starts releasing melatonin, and that's one signal that it's time to sleep. Now, during adolescence, something interesting happens: the timing of melatonin release shifts later, sometimes by two hours or more. So a fifteen-year-old who isn't sleepy at ten p.m. isn't necessarily being stubborn. Their body clock is genuinely running later. The problem is that school usually starts early. A teenager whose body wants to sleep from midnight to nine is being woken up at six-thirty. During the week, they build up what researchers call sleep debt, and then on weekends they sleep until noon to pay it back. Shifting your sleep schedule by several hours between weekdays and weekends has a name: social jet lag. It's as if you flew across several time zones every Friday and flew back every Monday. Some school districts have experimented with later start times, and the results have been fairly consistent: students get more sleep, and attendance improves. Grades improve too, though more modestly. Critics point out that later starts can cause problems with bus schedules and after-school sports, and those concerns are real. But the biology itself isn't really in dispute.

Today we're talking about caves. Many caves form in a kind of rock called limestone. Limestone is soft compared with many other rocks. When rain falls, it picks up a small amount of gas from the air and the soil. This makes the water a little acidic, a bit like very weak vinegar. As the water moves through cracks in the limestone, it slowly dissolves the rock. Over thousands of years, small cracks become large holes, and the holes become caves. Inside some caves, you can see shapes that hang from the ceiling, like icicles. These form when water drips and leaves tiny bits of rock behind. So water doesn't only make a cave. It also decorates it.

Let's look at how cities moved people before cars. In the eighteen-hundreds, many big cities had horse-drawn streetcars. These were like small buses that ran on metal rails in the street. The rails were important because a horse could pull a much heavier load on smooth rails than on a rough road. But horses had problems. They were expensive to feed, they got tired after a few hours, and they made the streets very dirty. So near the end of the century, cities began to replace them with electric streetcars. Electric streetcars were faster and cleaner, and they could run all day. Within about twenty years, horse-drawn streetcars had almost disappeared.

For most of history, earthquakes were treated as purely natural events, the result of stress building up along faults over centuries. But in recent decades, geologists have recorded a sharp rise in small and moderate earthquakes in regions that were once quiet, and in many cases the cause appears to be human activity. The main culprit isn't drilling itself, as people often assume. It's the disposal of wastewater. When oil and gas are extracted, huge volumes of salty water come up with them, and companies usually dispose of it by injecting it deep underground. Now, deep rock is full of faults, many of them already under stress but held in place by friction. Injected water raises the fluid pressure in the rock, which pushes the two sides of a fault slightly apart and reduces that friction. A fault that might have stayed locked for thousands of years can then slip. What makes this hard to manage is the delay. Pressure can spread for kilometers and take months or even years to reach a vulnerable fault, so by the time earthquakes start, the injection may have stopped long ago. Some regulators have limited injection volumes, and in those areas earthquakes have become less frequent, which, incidentally, is fairly strong evidence of a causal link.

When we picture medieval trade, we tend to imagine a merchant who owned his goods, sailed with them, and kept the profit. In practice, long-distance trade in the Mediterranean was often organized through a contract called the commenda. One partner, usually an older or wealthier investor, stayed at home and supplied the capital. The other, the traveling merchant, contributed little or no money but took the goods overseas, sold them, and bought cargo for the return voyage. When he came back, the profits were divided, typically three quarters to the investor and one quarter to the traveler. If the ship sank, the investor bore the financial loss, while the traveler lost only his time and effort, which, admittedly, on a sinking ship, might include his life. Why does this matter? Because it let people without capital enter trade. A young man with no money but good judgment could, after a few successful voyages, save enough to become an investor himself. Some historians argue that this mobility helped Venice and Genoa develop an unusually large merchant class. Others are more skeptical. They note that investors often chose relatives as their traveling partners, which would have limited how open the system really was.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Why We Feel Sleepy

Scientists often describe the timing of sleep with what is known as the two-process model. The first process, sometimes called sleep pressure, works like an hourglass. From the moment you wake up, a chemical called adenosine gradually accumulates in the brain, and the longer you stay awake, the stronger the urge to sleep becomes. Sleep clears the adenosine, resetting the hourglass. The second process is the circadian rhythm, an internal clock that runs on a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours, regardless of how long you have been awake.

The two processes usually work together, but they can also pull in opposite directions. This explains a common experience: people who stay up all night often feel more alert at dawn than they did at three in the morning, even though their sleep pressure is higher. The circadian clock, responding to the approaching day, sends a wake-up signal strong enough to partly offset the hourglass.

Caffeine interferes with the first process. It blocks the receptors that adenosine normally binds to, so the brain does not register the accumulated pressure. The adenosine is still there, however, which is why fatigue can return abruptly once the caffeine wears off.

Where Sand Comes From

Sand looks simple, but it has a long history. Most sand begins as part of a large rock, such as granite in a mountain. Over many years, rain, ice and wind break the rock into smaller and smaller pieces. Rivers then carry these pieces toward the sea. On the way, the pieces hit each other and become round and smooth. By the time they reach a beach, they are tiny grains. Not all sand is the same, however. Some beaches have white sand made from broken shells and coral, and some islands have black sand that comes from volcanic rock.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Paper Instead of Coins: The Bill of Exchange

Long-distance trade in medieval Europe faced a stubborn practical obstacle: moving coins. Silver and gold were heavy, attractive to thieves, and liable to be seized by the rulers whose territories merchants had to cross. By the thirteenth century, Italian merchants had devised an elegant alternative, the bill of exchange. A merchant in Florence could pay coins to a local banker and receive a written order instructing the banker's agent in, say, Bruges, to pay an equivalent sum in local currency some weeks later. The bill itself was worthless to a thief, since only the named recipient could collect the money.

The instrument had a second, less obvious function. The Church condemned usury, the charging of interest on loans, yet bankers needed to profit from the time their money was tied up. Because a bill involved converting one currency into another, bankers could build a margin into the exchange rate, and the interest was effectively concealed within the conversion. Contemporaries were not entirely deceived; theologians debated the legitimacy of such contracts for centuries. Nonetheless, the bill's ambiguity proved commercially indispensable, and its basic logic survives in the cheques and transfers of modern finance.

email.title: Write an Email
email.subject: Heating problem in Room 214, Ashford Hall
email.prompt:
You live in a university residence hall. For the past two weeks, the heater in your room has not worked properly, and the room is very cold at night. You submitted an online repair request ten days ago, but nobody has replied.

Write an email to the Campus Housing Office. In your email, do the following:
- Describe the problem with the heater.
- Explain how the problem is affecting you.
- Ask the office to take a specific action, and say when you are available.

Use full sentences, and write as much as you can.
email.rubric: Task: email to a university housing office about an unresolved repair. Must cover all 3 bullets: (1) describe the heater problem, (2) explain its effect on the writer (sleep, study, health), (3) request a specific action (repair visit, temporary heater, room move) and give availability. Look for polite but firm register, greeting and sign-off, mention of the earlier unanswered request, clear organization, accurate grammar and natural phrasing. Typical strong length 100-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, do these two things.
- State your view and back it up.
- Add something new to the thread, in your own words.
Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Moreau
professor.text: Many cities struggle with traffic and air pollution. One proposal is to make public transit completely free for everyone, paid for through local taxes. Others argue that the money would be better spent on improving service, for example by running buses more often and building new lines, while keeping fares. If the goal is to get more people out of their cars, which approach do you think would work better, and why?

students.name: Lena
students.text: I support free transit. Even a small fare makes people hesitate, especially low-income residents who need transit the most. If riding the bus costs nothing, people will at least try it, and many will keep using it once they see how convenient it is.

students.name: Tomás
students.text: I think better service matters more. Most people drive because the bus is slow or unreliable, not because it is expensive. If a bus comes only every half hour, making it free will not change much. Frequent, fast service is what actually competes with a car.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear opinion on free transit vs. better service, specific support (examples, reasons, consequences), engagement with Lena's or Tomás's point rather than repeating it, coherence, varied accurate grammar and vocabulary.

interview.title: Take an Interview
interview.instructions: An interviewer will ask you four questions. There is no preparation time. Answer each question and use the whole time to say as much as you can.
interview.context: You are joining a research study about sleep and daily routines. A researcher will ask you some questions in a short online interview.

items.text: Thank you for joining me today. To start, could you describe your usual sleep schedule on a typical weekday?
Many people say their sleep changes during busy periods, like exams or deadlines at work. How does your sleep change when you are under pressure, and how does that affect you?
Some people believe that using phones and computers late at night is the main reason young people don't get enough sleep. Do you agree? Why or why not?

Last question. Some companies now let employees choose their own working hours, so that they can sleep according to their natural rhythm. Do you think this should become more common, even if it makes it harder for teams to meet? Please explain your view.
